item.title: GOP starts coming to terms with a lame-duck Donald Trump
item.description: A Election Day “shellacking,” one GOP lawmaker said, will have the president “looking for our help more than we’d be looking for his.”

media:content.media:title: Trump, seen among Senate leaders during a June visit to the Capitol, could see quick tests of his post-election influence.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney and Mia McCarthy
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney and Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump will have his ironclad grip on congressional Republicans tested like never before if the party loses one or both chambers Tuesday.

Trump already appears to be gearing up to blame others if Democrats retake the House or the Senate. But within the halls of the Capitol, GOP lawmakers are contemplating whether the president’s ability to bend them to his whims will diminish if the party is swept out of power.

“We’ll see,” Rep. Lloyd Smucker (R-Pa.) said when asked how much influence the president will have after the midterms, before praising Trump’s record and willingness to hit the campaign trail on behalf of Republican candidates.

Granted anonymity to speak frankly before the election, many of the 15 GOP lawmakers interviewed about the future of Trump’s influence said they believe his days of dictating outcomes with Truth Social posts and late-night phone calls could be coming to an end.

“It's not like his persuasion is growing,” said a Republican senator. “Political capital is earned and lost the same way.”

One House Republican cast the potential fight for minority leader as an early test of Trump’s sway: “One would say that the president would have quite a bit of influence on who leads in the minority. But one would also say that he has less influence because some people would blame him” for a loss.

The member added: “That will be an interesting dynamic after Election Day. No one expects Trump to take any blame after the election. So if he doesn't, who does?”

It’s hardly the first time Republicans have predicted that Trump’s days of dominating the GOP were on the wane. A broad swath of the party turned on him after the Capitol attack on Jan. 6, 2021, only to come back to the fold as he regained power.

Despite plenty of kvetching publicly and privately about some of Trump's policies and personnel picks since being sworn in for a second term, most in the party have fallen in line — and few expect him to change his high-pressure style during his final two years in office.

Many Republicans anticipate he'll weigh in on 2028 congressional primaries while also playing a loud role in determining the party’s presidential nominee — as well as weighing in on day-to-day machinations on Capitol Hill.

“He’s going to continue fully engaged … regardless of the outcome,” Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso said in an interview, praising Trump’s “very creative” and “thoughtful” ideas on domestic and foreign affairs.

Rep. Chris Smith (R-N.J.) said in an interview “it'll be challenging” for Trump if Republicans lose the House but said his influence would persist: “He still has the bully pulpit, and I say that in a good way.”

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said Trump “is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.”

But unlike Trump’s last midterm drubbing, in 2018, a decisive loss this time would officially usher him into lame-duck status. While House members will all be campaigning for reelection with Trump still in office — and face the prospect of a presidential primary threat — only about a third of currently sitting Republican senators are in the same boat.

The rest will stand for reelection in 2030 and 2032, after Trump is out of office.

One GOP senator pointed to the party’s stable of vulnerable candidates and incumbents who have broken with Trump over the Iran conflict as a sign of things to come if Republicans take a battering Tuesday.

“He’s in trouble,” the senator said.

Another House Republican added that if Democrats win only a small majority in that chamber, Trump will “still carry a lot of sway.” But a “shellacking,” the lawmaker said, will have Trump “looking for our help more than we’d be looking for his.”

“If it’s truly a big blue wave, every committee will investigate the hell out of him the next two years and R’s will quickly start looking at [2028] and beyond,” the member added in a text message.

Trump will face a series of quick tests after the midterms. The House is expected to vote on whether to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth soon after members return. Some Republicans said if voters deliver a wipeout for their party amid widespread dissatisfaction with the Iran war, several of their colleagues could end up supporting the measure.

The president could also face headwinds if he tries to muscle a final party-line spending bill through Congress before Democrats take charge in either chamber and kill any chance for partisan legislation like the election bill known as the SAVE America Act. Republicans have already struggled to move these measures, and GOP lawmakers who just lost reelection could have little reason to rally behind them on their way out the door.

House Republicans are in particular keeping their eyes on whether Trump will weigh in on the GOP leadership races that will play out in the week after the election.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan of Ohio are expected to clash if Republicans are electing a minority leader. But many GOP lawmakers think Speaker Mike Johnson could have a shot at hanging on as the chamber's top Republican if Trump wants it.

Jordan and Scalise are also both close Trump allies, and most Republicans are skeptical he would choose between the two.

“The president of the United States certainly has influence,” Jordan said in an interview. “I think he'll continue to have influence.”

In the Senate, conservatives are privately questioning whether Trump will blame Senate Majority Leader John Thune if Republicans lose control of the chamber.

Trump sowed doubt about Thune’s leadership over the summer as he stewed about the Senate’s failure to act on the elections bill. But he more recently publicly defended Thune during the party’s midterm convention in September.

Many Republican senators expect Thune to keep his job even if Trump moves against him. Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) has aired frustrations about how the Senate is run but has repeatedly said he won’t run for leader and has declined to criticize Thune. Some GOP senators have privately speculated about whether Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) has leadership ambitions, but few think he’s actually interested.

Trump turning on Thune “certainly would not” cause Thune to lose his leadership race, said one of the GOP senators, adding that it was “absolutely the case” that Thune would keep his job even if Trump balks.

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), who is in line to run the Senate GOP campaign arm in the next Congress, said of Thune, “I don't think there's an insurgent movement that's against him.”

Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican, is backing Thune as well. Asked about the speculation that Trump could turn on Thune, Barrasso said, “He’s going to get reelected as leader.”

item.title: ‘Look what I brought home for you’: GOP embraces earmark revival as Election Day looms
item.description: Republican lawmakers in the country’s tightest races are bragging about “bringing home the bacon” to a sour electorate.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Bill Huizenga departs a vote at the U.S. Capitol on April 29, 2025.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
With voters sour on Republican governance, GOP candidates in the most competitive House and Senate races are reaching for a time-tested message that has grown out of fashion in their party: bringing home the federal bacon.

A POLITICO analysis of the dozen closest congressional races for Republican incumbents revealed that most are highlighting earmark success stories in the final days before voters head to the polls.

The ability to secure federal funding for pet projects back home — something many in the GOP have spent years trying to curtail — has given those candidates a positive talking point as President Donald Trump’s flagging approval ratings and widespread voter dissatisfaction over issues like the Iran war, high gas prices and tariffs weigh on other messages.

“When the president's job approval is in the 30s, it is helpful for Republican candidates to be able to create some distance from the president. It's challenging to do that without encouraging the president's wrath,” Republican pollster Whit Ayres said in an interview. “But focusing on bringing home the bacon might be one very good way to do it without antagonizing the president.”

In Michigan, Rep. Tom Barrett is out with an ad about a $750,000 earmark for youth mentoring; in New York, Rep. Mike Lawler is talking about how he secured $120 million for local projects.

Rep. Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania is telling voters he has “brought back more than $110 million to our community,” including millions in earmarks, while Rep. David Valadao has run ads showcasing $500 million in earmarks for water projects in California’s Central Valley.

Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, a GOP moderate seeking to project independence from Trump in a competitive contest, has repeatedly touted the exact count of the earmarks she has locked in over the last half-decade for her home state of Maine.

The sum: 672 projects totaling $1.5 billion, “from Madawaska to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford,” as she said in her opening statement earlier this month in her first debate against Democrat Troy Jackson. This past week, Collins has peppered voters with county-specific text messages detailing how much she’s secured for each area.

There are countless other examples of earmark campaigning among vulnerable Republican incumbents, though many conservatives remain reluctant to associate themselves with the practice. It still carries a stigma of corruption after two Republicans were sent to prison on related bribery charges in the mid-2000s, paving the way for the GOP to do away with earmarks in 2011.

That left GOP candidates unable to play up the clearest spoils of incumbency ahead of the “blue wave” of 2018. But Democrats revived them in 2021 with new safeguards, and now Republicans are taking advantage as they navigate another tough midterm cycle.

“That word ‘earmark’ can carry some negative baggage, especially among the old fiscal conservatives,” nonpartisan pollster Mike Noble said in an interview. “But when you describe that same expenditure as funding for a local water system, highway, public safety project — voters evaluate that differently.”

Recognizing the advantages, Republicans opted to keep earmarks around under unified party leadership in 2025, resulting in the enactment of almost $16 billion worth of earmarks this year. For those who still consider earmarks anathema to the GOP’s values of fiscal restraint, it’s causing complications on the trail.

Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga of Michigan is fielding criticism for not requesting any earmarks for his district. While he airs ads calling himself “tight with a buck,” his opponents are telling voters that lawmakers like Huizenga are increasing their net worth “while turning down community project funding.”

Some recent polling shows Huizenga trailing his Democratic challenger, state Sen. Sean McCann, by 1 percentage point.

McCann said in an interview he will “go to bat” for earmarks if he defeats Huizenga: “That's an expectation that people have when you want to represent them — that you do the things that are important and secure crucial investments for the district.”

Huizenga defended himself in a statement, saying “earmarks have a long history of waste and abuse by politicians looking to enrich themselves in office.”

Huizenga noted that he has “helped secure hundreds of millions in federal investments for Southwest Michigan without requesting a single earmark,” including a $400 million grant last year for a nuclear power plant and $51 million for a housing redevelopment project.

He isn’t the only Republican incumbent in a tight race who has foregone earmarks. Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is facing a competitive challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, refused to request cash for district-specific projects as part of the annual government funding process. Instead, he points to his support for efforts made possible through the 2021 infrastructure law signed by then-President Joe Biden, as well as other legislation and grants the Trump administration doles out for local efforts.

Trump officials have traveled to Alaska in recent weeks to stand alongside Sullivan in announcing the delivery of hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding for the state, including $38 million in energy grants and $250 million for rail infrastructure.

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who appears to be in a dead heat with his Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, also didn’t ask for any federal funding this year. But he is getting flak for seeking a $4.2 million earmark in 2024 to finance improvements to increase water to a wildlife refuge that borders his ranch.

Spokespeople for the Sullivan and Marshall campaigns did not respond to requests for comment.

Whether voters perceive earmark requests as positive or negative likely depends heavily on how a candidate frames the talking point, Noble said, acknowledging that incumbents rarely use the word in campaign ads or town hall speeches and instead speak broadly about how they “deliver” for their district.

“Voters, at the end of the day — it's about direct benefit. What are they getting out of this deal? That's one of the powers of incumbency. They have that ability to say, ‘Hey, look what I brought home for you,’” he said. “But again, what else are they going to talk about?”

item.title: Senate Democrats’ top super PAC spends in South Carolina for the first time
item.description: Senate Majority PAC is running digital ads in support of Democrat Annie Andrews in her race against GOP Sen. Darline Graham.

media:content.media:title: South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews greets supporters after speaking at a Town Hall campaign event at Seene Coffee on Oct. 29, 2026, in Summerville, South Carolina.

item.dc:creator: By Lisa Kashinsky and Alec Hernandez
item.dc:contributor: By Lisa Kashinsky and Alec Hernandez
item.content:encoded:
Senate Democrats’ top super political action committee is pushing into South Carolina — just five days before the election.

Senate Majority PAC is putting $750,000 into digital ads to boost Democrat Annie Andrews, who they see as in an increasingly competitive position against GOP Sen. Darline Graham. The first spot could air as soon as Friday, and is set to attack Graham over rising costs and position Andrews as a fighter against corruption, according to plans shared first with POLITICO.

The Chuck Schumer-aligned group’s investment comes as public polling shows a tightening race in the closing stretch. Republicans say they’re confident in Graham’s ability to hold the seat, in part because the GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund recently pledged to spend at least $5 million in the race. President Donald Trump has already held two rallies in the state to boost his hand-picked senator.

“South Carolina is tightening, and Republicans know it — you don’t send $5 million and the president to a state if you're not nervous,” SMP spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement.

“Darline Graham is an empty suit who was handed a Senate seat and has no idea what to do with it,” French added. “Annie Andrews will lower costs on gas, groceries, insurance, and housing. In a race this close, a late infusion of cash can make the difference, and that’s why we’re in.”

Representatives for Andrews and Graham did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the investment.

Even with the extensive outside support, Graham’s campaign has been weighed down by voter fatigue after several contentious primaries, questions about her political inexperience and an increasingly difficult national environment for Republicans.

The South Carolina spending marks Democrats’ newest late-stage push into deep-red Senate races as they look to leverage Americans’ frustrations with the cost of living and Trump’s agenda to keep expanding the map. If Andrews wins next week, it would mark the first time South Carolina elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998.

Strong showings by former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia have allowed SMP to draw down its spending in those erstwhile battlegrounds while pumping millions of dollars into traditionally red territories like Texas, Kansas and Mississippi.

item.title: Bill Foster cools on challenging Maxine Waters
item.description: Foster has been considering a bid to topple Waters as the top House Financial Services Democrat.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Bill Foster (D-Ill.) is weighing a challenge against Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) for the top Democratic spot on the House Financial Services Committee.

item.dc:creator: By Katherine Hapgood and Jasper Goodman
item.dc:contributor: By Katherine Hapgood and Jasper Goodman
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Bill Foster is leaning against challenging Rep. Maxine Waters for the top Democratic spot on the House Financial Services Committee, according to two people with knowledge of his thinking who were granted anonymity to discuss private deliberations.

The Illinois Democrat has been considering a bid to topple Waters but has not made a final decision, the people said. The timeline for him doing so is unclear.

Democratic Rep. Sean Casten, also from Illinois, told Waters earlier this month that he plans to run against her, likely teeing up a major fight over the Financial Services role, which the California Democrat has held since 2013.

Most Financial Services Democrats on the committee have publicly backed Waters for the role.

Foster, who was first elected in 2008, previously discussed with Waters ways to reform the committee that would give subcommittee chairs more power to shape the panel's agenda. A physicist with a doctorate, Foster is currently the top Democrat on a House Financial Services Financial Institutions Subcommittee.

A Foster spokesperson declined to comment.

item.title: Oklahoma’s next senator can be seated immediately after election, state AG rules
item.description: Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond ruled that Sen. Alan Armstrong’s appointment should end when the next senator is elected and before the current session of the Senate concludes on Jan. 3.

media:content.media:title: Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond is pictured, Feb. 1, 2023, during an interview in Oklahoma City.

item.dc:creator: By Ashley Ahn
item.content:encoded:
The winner of next week's Oklahoma Senate race will be able to take office immediately after the election, effectively ending Republican Sen. Alan Armstrong’s appointment before the current session of the Senate concludes, the state attorney general ruled on Thursday.

Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond’s ruling could pave the way for Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Okla.), the heavy favorite in the race and a Trump ally, to be seated by early November.

Armstrong, a former energy executive, was appointed in March to temporarily fill the seat vacated by Markwayne Mullin, now Department of Homeland Security secretary.

Both Armstrong and Hern submitted memorandums to the state attorney general’s office in disagreement over when Armstrong’s appointment ends, with Hern arguing he should be able to take office before the beginning of the next Congress.

"Oklahoma law and the U.S. Constitution point to the same answer: the voters fill this seat," Drummond said in a statement. "Oklahomans will choose their next senator at the polls on Nov. 3, and that person will be eligible to take office once the election is certified. This opinion gives the Governor and the Legislature clear guidance on how to proceed."

This November’s election is for a full six-year term in the Senate. Mullin, a former member of the House, initially won a 2022 special election to complete the term of the Sen. Jim Inhofe, who retired early in January 2023.

Armstrong was not a candidate to replace Mullin; Oklahoma law bars Senate appointees from seeking election to a full term.

Drummond’s formal opinion, addressed to Gov. Kevin Stitt and Oklahoma state Senate President pro tempore Lonnie Paxton, effectively sides with Hern and points to a state statute, which directs the governor to appoint a person “to serve in such office until a successor is elected.”

“The Governor has no discretion to decline or delay certifying the election,” Drummond added.

In a statement, the Hern campaign praised the state attorney general's decision. “We appreciate the Attorney General’s review and are pleased that his opinion confirms our understanding of Oklahoma law," it said.

A spokesperson for Armstrong’s office said they are reviewing the opinion, and that “in the meantime, Senator Armstrong’s full focus remains on passing comprehensive permitting reform to lower utility prices, grow the economy, and get America building again.”

item.title: This Reagan Republican is not amused
item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Campaigning in northwest Ohio this week, Speaker Mike Johnson took a shot at long-tenured Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur, saying, "I love the [Ronald] Reagan years, but I don't want to be serving with somebody who was there during the Reagan years."

One issue: There are two sitting Republicans who served under Reagan — Reps. Hal Rogers of Kentucky and Chris Smith of New Jersey.

Smith, who is now seeking a 24th term, told reporters Thursday he hadn't heard Johnson's comments but defended his record of legislative accomplishments as well as Reagan's honor.

"I don't know why he said that," Smith said, laughing. "I love Ronald Reagan. He was amazing."

item.title: Republican committee chair wants testimony from operatives accused of meddling in Alaska Senate race
item.description: Rep. James Comer wants transcribed interviews with the two individuals immediately after Election Day.

media:content.media:title: FILE - Mary Peltola, a Democrat running for the U.S. Senate seat in Alaska, addresses supporters at an election watch party on Aug. 18, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska. (AP Photo/Mark Thiessen, File)

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
House Oversight Chair James Comer said Thursday he’s launching an investigation into allegations that the campaign of former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Alaska, played a role in recruiting candidates with a similar name to her GOP opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, in order to confuse voters in Tuesday’s election.

The Kentucky Republican is requesting interviews with people allegedly involved in the plot: Elisa Rios, a former Peltola campaign staffer who spoke with the New York Times for the story that detailed Peltola’s alleged actions; and Jerid Kurtz, a Democratic political operative who, according to the Times, recruited people named Dan Sullivan to appear on the ballot.

Comer left open the possibility of issuing subpoenas if Rios and Kurtz do not comply with the transcribed interview requests. He’s also working fast, while his term as the committee’s top Republican culminates at the end of this year and the GOP majority could be lost to Democrats on Election Night: He wants Rios to appear before the committee on Nov. 5 and Kurtz on Nov. 6.

“Democrats are the party of fraud,” Comer said. “Knowing they can’t win on the issues, Democrats schemed to rig the U.S. Senate election in Alaska by deliberately confusing voters. This is part of a broader pattern of misconduct by today’s Democrat Party.”

Rios and Kurtz were not immediately reachable for comment.

The stakes are high for the Alaska Senate race that could decide the balance of power in the chamber — and more broadly in Congress. The Trump Justice Department has already laid the groundwork to challenge the election results if Peltola wins, on the basis that the presence of an independent candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, is an intentional push to mislead the voters; the incumbent senator’s middle initial is “S.”

Last week, the DOJ sued to prevent Alaska state officials from certifying the results should Sullivan lose: “Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Daniel J. Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan, and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity.”

In June, the Alaska Supreme Court allowed the independent Sullivan to stay on the ballot.

Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. Sullivan's campaign, said in a statement, "Alaskans deserve to know the truth, and the extent of Mary Peltola’s deception. As I’ve said all week, we will let these investigations run their course. One way or another, Alaskans will get the answers. We’re confident they can see through Mary Peltola’s shameful lies and manipulation."

Spokespeople for Peltola and the Oversight Committee’s top Democrat, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Capitol agenda: House Democrats’ next big battle
item.description: Progressives and moderates will both feel they have leverage to influence the legislative agenda if Democrats win control of the House next week.

media:content.media:title: Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) and Vice Chair Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) speak alongside other progressives outside the U.S. Capitol after an amendment to cut aide to Israel failed to pass the House on July 14, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
A battle of the competing factions of a potential House Democratic majority is already underway.

An expected wave of both progressives and moderates in the midterms has members of both contingents feeling strongly that any 2026 gains would be proof that their wing of the party should dictate the legislative agenda ahead of 2028.

In private phone calls, group chats and strategy sessions, the left flank is plotting out how to leverage its expanding ranks, while centrists are scheming about how to act as a counterbalance.

“There's going to be some real tension, because we have to move,” progressive Rep. Delia Ramirez of Illinois said in an interview. “Preserving perfect relationships with colleagues who don't feel the urgency the way that some of us feel it, because we live it every day, isn't my top priority. Protecting people is.”

The Congressional Progressive Caucus gathered incumbent and incoming members to Washington last month to strategize about how to advance their policy wishlist and to outline what Ramirez described as “nonnegotiables.”

Likely members of the new liberal cohort — which some are calling “The Bloc” — all campaigned on ending U.S. aid to Israel, abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and passing “Medicare for All.”

Because fewer progressives are running in competitive races this year, the left has had more breathing room to begin organizing its new members. But the more centrist collectives on Capitol Hill — like the New Democrat Coalition, Blue Dog Caucus and Problem Solvers Caucus — are hoping to quickly catch up and have already sketched out governing agendas that hew closely to the campaign messages coming from top party leaders.

“Just like with the progressives, there have been conversations among moderates about our policy priorities, with a clear proactive agenda,” said Rep. Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey, a veteran leader of the moderate wing. He said that he expects some of his colleagues on the left will push for “policy red lines that are too extreme and out of step with our Democratic values.”

Members of the New Dems published a65-page dossier in May pushing consensus bills that target lowering costs. And House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, on track to be speaker in a new Democratic majority, has already previewed an early slate of bills that align closely with their vision — rolling back Republican-led Medicaid cuts, restoring expired Affordable Care Act subsidies and ending President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Still, both moderates and progressives boast that they have Jeffries’ ear and have lobbied him in recent months to take up their priorities. 

What else we’re watching: 

— WARREN EYES LEADERSHIP MOVE: Sen. Elizabeth Warren doesn’t want to be Senate Democratic leader next year, but she is looking at taking on a bigger role after the midterms. A person familiar with the Massachusetts Democrat’s thinking, granted anonymity to speak candidly, says, “Warren will take a close look at Senate leadership opportunities, including the No. 3 slot.” Sen. Amy Klobuchar currently holds that spot but is expected to win next week’s race to be governor of Minnesota, creating a vacancy.

— A CONTESTED RACE FOR GOP CONFERENCE CHAIR?: Chatter is building around whether anyone will challenge House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan for her leadership slot next year. And, according to three people granted anonymity to share private conversations, some Republicans are hoping McClain’s previous opponent, Rep. Kat Cammack, gets into the race. Four House Republicans granted anonymity to speak candidly said they doubt Cammack will actually mount a challenge, but the Florida Republican isn’t ruling it out.

— COMPANIES PREPARE FOR DEMOCRATIC OVERSIGHT: A broad range of tech, finance, crypto and industrial companies, panicking over the likely onslaught of partisan investigations if Democrats retake Congress, are hiring lobbyists and crisis communications experts to gird against the potential deluge of inquiries. They’re also seeking outside legal counsel to help avoid reputational damage as Democrats promise to scrutinize private-sector dealings with the Trump administration.

Riley Rogerson, Jordain Carney, Mia McCarthy, Daniel Barnes and Oliver Ward contributed to this report.

item.title: Elizabeth Warren eyes post-election Senate leadership move
item.description: Warren, currently on the No. 5 rung, is looking to move up the Democratic Caucus ladder.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) speaks with reporters as she walks to a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 30, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Elizabeth Warren is looking at making a move within the Senate Democratic leadership team after the midterms.

Warren, who is currently in the No. 5 spot, isn’t interested in being top leader but could try to take on a bigger role on the caucus’ leadership team, according to a person with knowledge of her thinking who was granted anonymity to speak candidly.

“After the midterm elections, Warren will take a close look at Senate leadership opportunities, including the No. 3 slot,” the person said.

As Steering and Policy chair, Sen. Amy Klobuchar now holds the No. 3 spot in the caucus. But she’s expected to win the Minnesota governor’s race next week, which would leave the top tier of the Senate Democratic leadership team without a woman for the first time in a decade.

Former Sen. Debbie Stabenow previously held the third-ranked spot but retired. Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) also previously held the position but left leadership.

A spokesperson for Warren declined to comment. Her potential move comes as Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer is seeking reelection as leader and Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) is expected to move unopposed into the No. 2 role of whip. Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) is in the caucus’ No. 4 position.

It’s not clear if Booker, who is viewed as a potential 2028 White House contender, will try to move to a different spot next year. He currently chairs the Strategic Communications Committee, a position that gives him influence over caucus messaging strategy. A spokesperson declined to comment Wednesday.

Warren and Booker are friendly, and colleagues don’t expect them to run against each other in the upcoming shakeup. Democrats have generally avoided public leadership contests and instead work out titles and positions privately.

The title and responsibilities for the No. 3 position, as well as other posts, also could change as Democrats reshuffle things after the midterms. Leadership elections aren’t expected until early December.

A similar dynamic played out two years ago when both Booker and Klobuchar were eyeing the No. 3 gig, which at that point was overseeing Senate Democrats’ Policy and Communications Committee. As part of the deal, Klobuchar took the No. 3 spot as chair of a reconfigured Steering and Policy Committee, and Booker got the No. 4 spot with a portfolio tailored to his interest in messaging.

Warren joined the leadership team in 2014 alongside Senator Mark Warner of Virginia and has steadily climbed through the ranks to become a leading progressive voice in the Senate. She’s not planning a repeat run for president in 2028 and is instead focusing, in part, on helping drive the party’s economic policy. She’s also likely to chair the Senate Banking Committee if Democrats flip the majority next week.

Warren was also part of a group of senators who split with Schumer and the Senate Democratic campaign arm over their primary strategy during the current election cycle. But she’s also helped raise money for the party organs, including more than $1 million for the DNC online, according to a person with knowledge of DNC fundraising who was granted anonymity to disclose private figures.

She’s also raised more than $1 million for the DSCC and has been campaigning with candidates across the country. She’s visited several states in recent weeks including Michigan, Maine and New Hampshire, which all have battleground Senate and key House races.

item.title: The battle for the future of a House Democratic majority is raging
item.description: Rival factions are already plotting how they will wield influence in anticipation of a midterm victory.

media:content.media:title: House progressives, led by Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), recently ran a member retreat to make plans for a possible majority.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
The battle for the future of a House Democratic majority is already underway.

In phone calls, group chats and strategy sessions, competing wings of the party are jockeying for position, seeking to build unity, influence and governing agendas in advance of what they hope will be an Election Day romp.

The Congressional Progressive Caucus gathered incumbent and incoming members to Washington last month to prepare an agenda and discuss how they will use their leverage to advance it. Moderate Democrats are also scheming in behind-the-scenes conversations about how they can act as a counterbalance to the left with their own affirmative vision for the majority.

The early plotting sets up an inevitable clash between the factions — both of which are already arguing any midterm gains would be proof that their wing of the party should be standard-bearers ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

“There's going to be some real tension, because we have to move,” progressive Rep. Delia Ramirez of Illinois said in an interview. “Preserving perfect relationships with colleagues who don't feel the urgency the way that some of us feel it because we live it every day isn't my top priority. Protecting people is.”

Both sides are courting potential incoming members with offers of mentorship and campaign resources as they attempt to shore up their ranks.

Ramirez is mentoring an incoming batch of ultraprogressives, including Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York and Melat Kiros of Colorado, whom she recently hosted in Chicago to talk about shared priorities. All campaigned on ending U.S. aid to Israel, abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and passing “Medicare for All” universal health coverage, in addition to promoting economic populist policies like a minimum wage increase.

These presumptive members, many of whom identify as democratic socialists, have garnered outsize attention — some are calling them “The Bloc” — but the organizing effort has extended to a larger group of incoming progressives.

That outreach has included a September retreat run by the Congressional Progressive Caucus chair, Rep. Greg Casar of Texas, as well as other senior progressives such as Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington, a former CPC chair. The group strategized about how to maximize their influence to advance their wishlist and to settle on what Ramirez described as “non-negotiables.”

In a session on Medicare for All, for example, the progressives discussed pushing for a committee vote and Congressional Budget Office fiscal estimate on the policy as ways to build momentum around the issue ahead of a possible post-2028 Democratic trifecta.

Jayapal said the conversations centered on developing an “inside-outside strategy” that identifies points of leverage in the House — such as procedural votes and the drafting of a caucus rules package — to reflect “the voice of many of our new members who are coming in on fire.”

Moderates, meanwhile, are already wary of seeing routine House business weaponized for factional warfare, potentially threatening the reelection prospects of swing-district members. Members of overlapping centrist groups, including the New Democrat Coalition, the Blue Dog Caucus and Problem Solvers Caucus have discussed how to serve as a counterweight to the left.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey, a veteran leader of the centrist wing, said he was eyeing “concrete steps to stop socialists trying to jam the extremist parts of their agenda.”

“Just like with the progressives, there have been conversations among moderates about our policy priorities, with a clear proactive agenda,” Gottheimer said. “As expected, there will be policy red lines that are too extreme and out of step with our democratic values. Many of us are already talking to each about the importance of countering those extremist positions and focusing on issues more representative of the majority of Americans.”

“The good news: there are plenty of issues, frankly, that most Democrats agree on,” he added. “But there are places where you’ll see tension.”

Precisely how moderates plan to neutralize the party’s left flank remains a topic of live discussion among members and aides, who say a specific plan will depend on the outcome of the midterms. They are banking on a bumper crop of new pragmatic members from traditionally Republican territory to simply outnumber the “Bloc.”

“There is a lot of angst among some moderates about this DSA faction and squad expansion,” a senior moderate Democratic operative said in an interview. “The size of the majority will matter a lot.”

Each side is getting support from outside groups who are helping to develop policy plans and marshal grassroots support for their respective positions.

On the left, for instance, the Justice Democrats have convened meet-ups and are working to establish lines of communication between members. Centrist groups like Searchlight Institute and Third Way, meanwhile, are hosting their own meetings and cautioning Democrats against taking up certain hard-left positions.

“We see our role as, frankly, being kind of the hall monitor of the situation,” said Searchlight spokesperson Tré Easton. “Let's make sure that as Democrats are given the opportunity to govern, they remember why voters sent them to be there in the first place.”

Because fewer progressives are running in competitive races, the left has had more breathing room to begin organizing incoming members. But the centrist organs are hoping to quickly catch up and have already sketched out governing agendas that hew closely to the campaign messages coming from top party leaders.

The New Dems — the largest ideological bloc of House Democrats, with more than 110 members — published a 65-page dossier in May pushing broadly acceptable bills that target lowering costs.

Rep. Nikki Budzinski of Illinois, who is running unopposed to chair the group in the next Congress, said in an interview that the group’s size “will make us a force in determining the Democratic caucus's agenda” — with an eye on delivering on the campaign promises that incoming members made.

“We want to make sure that we're running and accomplishing the policy that they don't have to run from themselves back home,” she said. “That these are things that they can run toward.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has already previewed an early slate of bills that align with the New Dems’ vision — rolling back Republican-led Medicaid cuts, restoring expired Affordable Care Act subsidies and ending President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Jeffries has also taken steps to get his left and right flanks used to talking to each other and seeking compromise. This summer, he established five working groups, each led by a progressive and a moderate, to develop proposals to lower health care, housing, energy, child care and grocery costs.

He told reporters earlier this month that Democrats had made an “ironclad” promise to “focus on the affordability crisis and to drive down the high cost of living.”

“We intend to keep it, and it's what unites Democrats across the ideological spectrum,” he said.

Both moderates and progressives boast that they have Jeffries’ ear and have lobbied him in recent months to take up their priorities. But should Democrats fulfill internal expectations and win the majority, the speaker election looms as an initial flashpoint in the factional clash.

Although no alternative candidate has emerged, some incoming progressives have withheld commitments to supporting Jeffries as speaker, with many saying they want further “conversations” about the governing agenda — if not outright concessions.

For the centrists, support for Jeffries could be a litmus test: Rep. Greg Stanton of Arizona, who leads the New Democrats’ campaign arm, said in an interview that every single candidate the group endorsed supports Jeffries for speaker.

Kiros did not say in an interview if she would back Jeffries for speaker but she described a “wonderful” conversation with him about her top priorities: Medicare for All, a data center moratorium and Israel arms embargo.

She and other progressives have offered an olive branch to moderates, acknowledging there will be ways to work across the caucus — and even across the aisle — to pass law. Members of both wings have repeatedly raised passing a minimum wage hike.

“A big part of what the Progressive Caucus has been committed to doing has been to reforming the image of the Democratic Party back into a party that puts working class people first,” Casar said. “It means doing important outreach work to other parts of the Democratic Caucus.”

But leaders on the left said that working with moderates should not be confused with ditching the values they campaigned on.

Voters, Ramirez said, “are tired of nice little words and statements and letters, and they want to see us fight like hell for them.”

Mia McCarthy contributed to this report.

CORRECTION: A earlier version of a photo caption misidentified Rep. Greg Casar's party. He is a Democrat.

item.title: Top House Democrats demand Trump preserve conversations with Grok
item.description: Reps. Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia are signaling their interest in investigating the White House's use of AI chatbots.

media:content.media:title: Elon Musk and President Donald Trump take part in a press conference in the Oval Office at the White House, on May 30, 2025.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
The top Democrats on the House Judiciary and Oversight Committees want President Donald Trump to preserve his conversations with artificial intelligence chatbots as part of an inquiry into whether Elon Musk's AI assistant played a role in shaping White House policy — a preview of what’s to come if their party flips the chamber next week.

In a letter to Trump obtained by POLITICO, Reps. Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Robert Garcia of California are demanding that the president preserve “any prompts” submitted to AI chatbots, including Musk's Grok, OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude while “carrying out your constitutional, statutory, or other official or ceremonial duties,” along with the AI responses.

Raskin and Garcia — who are expected to wield the Judiciary and Oversight gavels if Democrats win back the House, respectively — are also asking for a briefing on the matter by 5:00 p.m. on Nov. 11.

Their request was informed by reporting that said Trump sought Grok’s “advice on carrying out some of your presidential duties, including asking Grok to opine on how Venezuelans would respond to the capture of President Nicolás Maduro.” The lawmakers note that, just “weeks later,” Trump “ordered the U.S. military, without congressional authorization, to attack Venezuela and capture President Maduro.”

Garcia and Raskin called the example “deeply troubling” because Trump “consulted Grok — but not Congress — on your military deployment to Venezuela, circumventing Congress’s constitutional power to declare war and introducing instead into American foreign policy decision making a technology that is highly manipulable and demonstrably error-prone.”

They also said the use of AI chatbots by the White House “exposes the United States to acute national security risks” and that usage “exposes the country to malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties.”

A White House official said in a statement that "the White House preserves all required records in accordance with the law."

Musk did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: ‘Lisa is Lisa’: Murkowski endorses a Democrat as she faces 2028 dilemma
item.description: Alaska insiders say it’s not necessarily a hint: “She doesn’t make decisions based on party.”

media:content.media:title: Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) emerges from a Senate Republican Conference luncheon at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 24, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney, Lisa Kashinsky and Riley Rogerson
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney, Lisa Kashinsky and Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski endorsed a Democrat for governor this week as she ponders her own reelection decision. Amid speculation about her retirement, political operatives and longtime watchers say it’s not necessarily a clue as to what she’s thinking.

Murkowski backed Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins to lead her home state Tuesday, saying that he would “serve all Alaskans, regardless of party.”

Her decision is a break with her party, which has three candidates in the four-way ranked choice general election next week. President Donald Trump has backed GOP candidate Bernadette Wilson to succeed outgoing GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy.

It could be read by some as an indication that Murkowski might be contemplating retirement rather than seeking reelection in 2028 — or positioning herself to win by appealing across the aisle, as she has done in the past. Trump has repeatedly lashed out at the senator and could rally Alaska Republicans to oust her.

But back home, her move to endorse a Democrat who is promising to work productively with state legislators of both parties is being viewed as further evidence of her well-known independent streak rather than tea leaves to be read about her own race.

“It’s certainly no surprise. Lisa is Lisa. She doesn’t make decisions based on party,” said Art Hackney, a GOP operative in Alaska running a super PAC for Sen. Dan Sullivan. “She’s looked at the four candidates and decided JKT is the best choice.”

Longtime Alaska political aide and journalist Larry Persily also said in an interview that he does not think Murkowski’s endorsement is a “signal for 2028.”

He called the move “the indication of her frustration with the current [Dunleavy] administration,” adding that she “doesn't want to see anything close to a repeat. I think it's a realization that her voice matters in Alaska.”

She hasn’t made a decision about running for reelection and has said little publicly about her thinking. Spokespeople for Murkowski did not respond to a question Wednesday about her endorsement or her 2028 decision.

It’s not the first time Murkowski has endorsed a Democrat. While she is backing Sullivan in his current battleground Senate race, she previously backed his Democratic rival, then-Rep. Mary Peltola, in the at-large House race. Murkowski’s father, former U.S. senator and former Gov. Frank Murkowski, is also backing Kreiss-Tomkins.

Further evidence of Lisa Murkowski’s independence was on display this week surrounding the 2026 Senate race — and allegations that Democrats schemed to put a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot to confuse voters.

After the Justice Department filed a lawsuit last week to block certification, citing the two Sullivans on the ballot, Murkowski pushed back in a statement, saying “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates.”

Then, after the New York Times published evidence Wednesday that Peltola’s campaign and national Democratic operatives had knowledge of the plans, Murkowski spoke out again to say Peltola and her campaign needed to share the “honest truth” about “a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials.”

Trump, meanwhile, has renewed his attacks on Murkowski, calling her the “worst senator” in a Truth Social post over the weekend following her criticism of the DOJ lawsuit.

Murkowski and Trump are also on opposite sides when it comes to Alaska’s ranked choice voting system, which eliminates traditional party primaries. Trump has blasted the state’s system as “corrupt,” pointing to the three Republicans on the ballot in the governor’s race compared to one Democratic candidate.

Alaska is one of only two states that use ranked choice voting statewide, and there is a referendum on this year’s ballot to repeal it. Some have credited the system for helping Murkowski defeat a challenger from her right in 2022.

Though Murkowski votes with her party most of the time, she’s been willing to break with the administration on key foreign and domestic policy questions and has voted against some of Trump’s Cabinet picks, including Todd Blanche’s nomination earlier this year to be attorney general.

Some Senate Republicans have privately questioned if Murkowski will run for reelection and, if she does, whether Trump will recruit another Republican to run against her. Murkowski defeated a Trump-backed challenger in 2022 after already pulling off a legendary electoral feat in 2010 by losing the GOP primary then winning the general election via a write-in campaign.

Heading into a 2028 race, Dunleavy has garnered months of speculation as a potential Senate candidate. But he has been dogged by low approval ratings and poor relations with other Alaska Republicans.

Murkowski said this week she has “found fault with the Dunleavy administration” and that it had “federal money on the table.”

After Fox News reported last year Dunleavy would challenge Murkowski, a spokesperson for the governor said in a statement that Dunleavy was “focused on moving Alaska forward during the remainder of his second term.” Spokespeople for Dunleavy did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday about Murkowski’s fresh criticism of his administration.

National Republican political operatives who were granted anonymity to speak candidly speculated that Dunleavy could be more interested in a potential Cabinet spot than a Senate seat if he decides to stay in politics.

Trump has repeatedly praised Dunleavy, including at a Sept. 30 White House event where he said he was a “great governor and a friend of mine.”

item.title: TV station says it is ‘pulling’ GOP ad attacking Pennsylvania House candidate
item.description: President Donald Trump’s No Going Back PAC targets Democrat Janelle Stelson over an unsubstantiated allegation.

media:content.media:title: Democrat Janelle Stelson speaks at a campaign event in her race against Republican U.S. Rep. Scott Perry of Pennsylvania, Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026, in York Haven, Pa.

item.dc:creator: By Riley Rogerson
item.content:encoded:
A Harrisburg-area television station said it is “pulling” a controversial advertisement attacking Pennsylvania House candidate Janelle Stelson, who is locked in one of the country’s tightest House races.

The ad is sponsored by No Going Back, a group affiliated with the President Donald Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. super PAC. The ad raises an unsubstantiated public nudity allegation which Stelson — a longtime local broadcast journalist — denies. The PAC has spent $295,000 on the ad, which has aired on multiple local stations since Oct. 25, according data from ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

Stelson is facing Republican Rep. Scott Perry in the south-central Pennsylvania district. The No Going Back ad, and a similar spot from Perry’s campaign, have sparked significant local attention in the days before the election.

While it is typical for officials to litigate campaign ads, it is highly unusual that television stations actually pull them down. A spokesperson for the DCCC said this would be the first time this cycle that a campaign ad has been pulled by a station

“We will continue to pursue every possible legal avenue to combat these verifiably false attacks that fail to meet the already miserably low standard of ethics Scott Perry has set for himself,” Stelson campaign manager Alma Baker said in a statement. “Perry should take the rest of his lying ads off the air.”

In a letter sent to stations airing the ad this week, lawyers for Stelson’s campaign and House Democrats’ campaign arm called the ad “false and defamatory” and demanded that it be taken down.

In a Wednesday morning email reviewed by POLITICO, the general sales manager for ABC affiliate WHTM, Michael Nurse, informed lawyers that the station was “pulling the ad in question out of rotation as soon as we can” and noting the station did not receive a response from the advertising agency that placed the order.

As of this story’s publication, however, the ad continued to air.

In another email reviewed by POLITICO, a representative for WGAL — the Harrisburg NBC affiliate where Stelson worked for over 25 years — said that they are “not airing” the ad.

Reached by phone, Nurse declined to comment. Other WHTM officials as well as spokespeople for WGAL did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

A spokesperson for the Perry campaign referred a reporter to No Going Back PAC to answer questions about the ad. When reached for comment, a spokesperson for MAGA, Inc. shared two Oct. 28 letters from the super PAC’s attorney, Andrew Murphy, to local station managers and cable system operators saying “ad is true and must remain in rotation.”

Aaron Pellish contributed to this report.

item.title: Pelosi in London
item.dc:creator: By Dan Bloom
item.content:encoded:
LONDON — Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi was spotted at the U.K. House of Common Wednesday, watch Britain's new leader, Andy Burnham, at Prime Minister's Questions. Perched up in the special galleries near political journalists, she studied the order of questions intently in between chatting to a top editor from the Daily Express.

Sadly for Pelosi, she didn't have the best seat in the house — she was facing Opposition Leader Kemi Badenoch over the top of Burnham's head — and she left midway through the main event of the day, Chancellor John Healey's budget speech.

item.title: Capitol agenda: House GOP eyes Jordan vs. Scalise
item.description: If Republicans lose the House next week, some GOP lawmakers are skeptical Speaker Mike Johnson would stay on as the top Republican in the chamber.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jim Jordan speaks to attendees at the 3rd Annual Freedom Fry, hosted by South Carolina Rep. Russell Fry on Oct. 26, 2026, in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
House Republicans are coming to terms with the fact they could lose their majority next week and be launched into a nasty leadership race.

Speaker Mike Johnson recently signaled he could stay on as GOP leader in the minority. But interviews with three dozen GOP lawmakers and senior Republican aides reveal most are skeptical Johnson runs in that scenario. They’re keeping a close eye on two potential alternatives: Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise.

The two men are being careful not to acknowledge any jockeying in the final lead-up to the midterms, but many Republicans expect the contest to explode into plain view after Tuesday. Candidates only have until Nov. 6 to declare their intentions to run in the Nov. 10 GOP leader elections.

Scalise, after spending nearly eight years as the No. 2 House Republican, has raised scads of money and built back-slapping relationships with a broad cross-section of members.

But he is facing a squeeze if Dems win the majority: Rep. Tom Emmer intends to run for the party whip regardless of the outcome, which is the No. 2 spot in the minority. If Johnson were to try to stay on in that scenario, Scalise would be forced into a contested race to either move up or keep his rung on the GOP power ladder.

Scalise said in an interview that “anybody who’s measuring the drapes of the minority leader’s office is not focused on the right things.”

The math for a potential minority leader bid runs in Jordan’s favor: He needed near-unanimity to win a race for speaker — which he lost in 2023. But elections for minority leader involve Republicans voting among themselves, and the Ohio Republican has made conspicuous moves to build support with different factions of the party.

In an interview from the campaign trail in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, Jordan said he’s “helping anybody, everybody,” and encouraging the GOP to “stick together.”

While Jordan and Scalise are being most closely watched for the No. 1 post, some believe Emmer could emerge as a candidate if others fail, as could Texas Rep. August Pfluger. Many will also be keeping eyes on President Donald Trump, who has yet to weigh in on the post-election GOP leadership picture.

Still, many, though not all, predict that a Republican midterm wipeout could leave members reluctant to elevate a member of the existing leadership structure and instead choose a known face of the conservative insurgency.

“It’s Jordan’s race to lose,” said a House Republican granted anonymity to speak candidly about the as-yet-unofficial race. “I think it’s his time.”

What else we’re watching: 

— TRUMP’S RUSSIA EMBRACE FALLOUT: Trump may have finally alienated the faction key to delivering his colossal defense budget: Republican hawks. The president — relying on the reconciliation process — will need almost unanimous support from Senate and House Republicans to enact his $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget after the midterm elections, especially if the GOP is about to lose one or both chambers of Congress. But Trump’s recent receptiveness to Russia has alarmed the very people pushing for more military spending. And they warn that his agenda won’t survive if the embrace of Moscow continues.

— OIL STATE DEMOCRAT REVIVAL? Next week’s midterm elections could usher in the revival of a rare type of politician: Democratic senators representing states rich in fossil fuels — and Republicans. Moderate Democrats view potential wins from Senate candidates like James Talarico of Texas and Mary Peltola of Alaska as a way to broaden the party’s tent on energy issues heading into what’s expected to be a competitive 2028 election cycle. It could also challenge the sway environmental groups have had with the party in recent decades.

Mia McCarthy, Meredith Lee Hill, Connor O’Brien, Mark Satter and Pavan Acharya contributed to this report.

item.title: The race the House GOP can’t stop talking about: Jim Jordan vs. Steve Scalise
item.description: As top leaders preach optimism, rank-and-file Republicans contemplate a nasty race for minority leader.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Jim Jordan, right, seen with Rep. Russell Fry, said Republicans need to "stick together" at a Oct. 26 GOP rally in Myrtle Beach, S.C.

item.dc:creator: By Mia McCarthy and Meredith Lee Hill
item.dc:contributor: By Mia McCarthy and Meredith Lee Hill
item.content:encoded:
MYRTLE BEACH, South Carolina — Donald Trump is facing his worst-ever approval ratings as president, GOP candidates in deep-red districts are scrambling for political cover, and Jim Jordan would like his fellow House Republicans to know he’s here to help.

“We are helping anybody, everybody,” the veteran Ohio lawmaker said in an interview on the sidelines of a get-out-the-vote rally in South Carolina, a typically red state that is suddenly a midterm battleground.

The differences between Republicans “are pretty darn small compared to the differences in Republicans and the radicals who control the other party,” Jordan added, “so let's stick together.”

To the outside ear, that might sound like generic campaign-trail hokum. But to Jordan’s colleagues, his comments essentially renouncing the factional warfare that made him a proto-MAGA star is emblematic of the shadow election battle that is now quietly underway — to lead what is expected to be a diminished House Republican Conference.

Interviews with three dozen GOP lawmakers and senior Republican aides revealed the widespread expectation that their House majority is coming to an end and that many are skeptical Speaker Mike Johnson would run for minority leader in that scenario.

They are keeping a close eye on two potential alternatives — Jordan, who has run twice before to lead House Republicans, and Majority Leader Steve Scalise, who has spent more than a decade climbing the GOP leadership ladder.

While most expect the contest to explode into plain view after Tuesday’s election, neither man is acknowledging any jockeying — or even the possibility that the GOP could lose the majority.

“I'm supporting Hakeem Jeffries for minority leader,” Scalise scoffed in an interview, referring to the top House Democrat, and said that “anybody who's measuring the drapes of the minority leader's office is not focused on the right things.”

But their colleagues are closely following their respective pre-midterm maneuvers — including trips like Jordan’s — and quietly handicapping who might have the advantage if their expectations for an underwhelming Election Day come to pass.

Scalise has spent nearly eight years as the No. 2 leader, raising scads of money and building back-slapping relationships with a broad cross-section of members. He’s traveled this cycle with 203 candidates and incumbents and sent nearly $24 million to fellow Republicans. Jordan, meanwhile, has made himself into a conservative icon through his battles with top GOP leaders and his combative performances at Oversight and Judiciary committee hearings, only to take a more conciliatory turn in recent years.

Many, though not all, predict that a Republican wipeout Tuesday would leave members reluctant to elevate a member of the existing leadership structure and would instead choose a known face of the conservative insurgency.

“It’s Jordan’s race to lose,” said a House Republican, who like others in this story was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the as-yet-unofficial race. “I think it’s his time.”

“People want fresh blood,” another GOP member said — referring to the 62-year-old Jordan, not the 61-year-old Scalise.

Aside from the election results, the big unknown surrounds Johnson, who just celebrated his three-year anniversary as speaker. He recently suggested in a CBS News interview that he believed his “colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference” even in the minority — something no former speaker has done since Nancy Pelosi’s Democrats lost the 2010 midterms.

A close election result could make that tenable, but most Republicans believe he will step aside. Retiring Rep. Mark Amodei (R-Nev.) said in an interview he’s told Johnson he “sincerely” wants him to stay on as speaker next Congress but acknowledged the current national landscape is not “warm” for Republicans.

“When … everything's good, the quarterback's the hero,” Amodei said. “When you lose, I'm sure there'll be plenty of blame to go around — that's what transpires.”

Asked if he would back Johnson for the top spot regardless of Tuesday’s results, Scalise said, “I support Mike for speaker, and I want to see us, again, work and leave everything out on the field.”

A Johnson spokesperson said the speaker is “solely focused on holding the majority” and plans to campaign in 21 districts across 13 states before Election Day. If he succeeds in staving off Democrats, most Republicans believe those in the existing leadership slate would continue in their posts. The speaker raised $526 million this cycle for House Republican campaigns and the major House GOP super PAC.

If Democrats win the majority, Scalise is facing a squeeze: Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the current No. 3, has said regardless of the election outcome he will run for party whip — which is the No. 2 spot in the minority. If Johnson were to try to stay on in that scenario, Scalise would be forced into a contested race to either move up or keep his rung on the GOP power ladder.

The initial hours after a GOP loss could see a flurry of announcements as potential leaders make their intentions known and scramble to win verbal commitments from their colleagues. Candidates have only until Nov. 6 to declare, with the leadership election scheduled for the Tuesday after the midterms.

While Jordan and Scalise are being most closely watched, some believe Emmer could emerge as a candidate if others fail, as could Texas Rep. August Pfluger, the outgoing chair of the Republican Study Committee.

Many will also be keeping eyes on President Donald Trump, who has yet to weigh in on the post-election GOP leadership picture. He endorsed Johnson for reelection Monday without mentioning him continuing as top leader.

White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said Trump is “laser-focused on maintaining Republican majorities in Congress” and is “certainly not weighing in on Hakeem’s race and possible Democrat challengers for Minority Leader.”

Were he to mount a minority leader run, Jordan would have to overcome a pair of previous failed bids for the No. 1 post — where, in both cases, colleagues saw him as too combative and ideological to lead the party.

His 2018 run for minority leader, in the aftermath of the last Democratic House takeover, fell well short to Kevin McCarthy. He went on to ally himself with McCarthy, however, and mounted a bid to take over as speaker in 2023 after McCarthy was ousted from the post.

So did Scalise, who beat him in an initial conference tally, but neither man could gather the required 218 votes — ultimately leading to Johnson’s election as speaker. What many Republicans remember most about the process was a scorched-earth campaign conducted by Jordan’s allies outside of Congress, with some members recalling floods of phone calls during the election drama — including some death threats.

Asked about those incidents, Jordan said, “There’s no place for that.”

“As a guy who gets death threats all the time, I don't want that to happen to anybody — Republican, Democrat, any American,” he said.

The math for a potential minority leader bid is different: Jordan needed near-unanimity to win the speaker race, which is contested among both parties on the House floor. Election as minority leader involves Republicans voting only among themselves, and Jordan has made conspicuous moves in the past three years to build support with more centrist members of the party.

He’s made campaign appearances for endangered members like Rep. Jen Kiggans of Virginia, lending the star power of a Fox News regular to their campaign stops. As Judiciary chair, Jordan sent signals to farm-state Republicans that he could be willing to back off his hard-line immigration stances and agree to new guest-worker measures aimed at the agricultural industry, according to three people involved in those conversations.

Jordan has also retained his backing from the more MAGA-friendly corners of the conference, including members who have clashed with McCarthy, Johnson and Scalise. He rallied Saturday in Clearwater, Florida, with one of them — Rep. Anna Paulina Luna.

In an interview, Luna credited Jordan with helping her get elected in 2022 and faulted the House’s existing leaders for standing in the way of her efforts to ban stock trading and allow new parents in the House to vote by proxy.

Asked about her potential support for a Jordan leadership run, Luna said he “definitely has a really good shot at it.”

“I am fair game for anyone who thinks that they have a shot at that position,” she added. “I want to hear what the platform is. But I will tell you that Jim Jordan helped get me elected, and I have an immense amount of respect for him because I remember who was there for me when no one else was.”

Kimberly Leonard contributed to this report.

CORRECTION: An earlier version of this article misidentified Steve Scalise's age. He is 61.

item.title: FBI raids Beverly Hills mansion tied to former Eric Swalwell donor
item.description: Federal authorities raided a home connected to Stephen Cloobeck, a billionaire and one-time associate of former Rep. Eric Swalwell, on Tuesday.

media:content.media:title: Stephen Cloobeck, a one-time California gubernatorial candidate, dropped his bid and donated more than $1 million to back Eric Swalwell after he declared his candidacy.

item.dc:creator: By Casey He
item.content:encoded:
The FBI on Tuesday raided a Los Angeles area mansion connected to Stephen Cloobeck, a billionaire and former Democratic donor who was a close associate of former Rep. Eric Swalwell.

“The FBI is executing a federal search warrant” at the Beverly Hills mansion, which is listed on Cloobeck’s California business filings, a spokesperson for the FBI’s Los Angeles field office said in a statement.

No arrests are planned, and the affidavit for the search warrant remains sealed, the spokesperson said. The FBI search was related to “an ongoing criminal investigation,” a Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement, declining to provide further details.

Cloobeck, a one-time California gubernatorial candidate, dropped his bid and donated more than $1 million to back Swalwell after he declared his candidacy. But he later said he had cut ties with the former lawmaker after sexual assault allegations against Swalwell emerged.

Swalwell resigned from Congress and dropped his gubernatorial bid but has denied the allegations. The Justice Department has launched a criminal investigation into Swalwell that included an FBI search of his Washington home in August, the AP reported at the time.

Cloobeck was arrested in May after Los Angeles County prosecutors charged him with allegedly attempting to impede victim or witness testimony. He was later released on bail and pleaded not guilty to all counts in August.

Cloobeck and his attorney did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A spokesperson for the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said it has not taken part in the FBI’s Tuesday raid.

item.title: Capitol agenda: Democrats face reckoning on trans issues
item.description: A party that ran on affordability would face a serious split in the majority.

media:content.media:title: A person holds a sign that says "TRANS KIDS BELONG" outside the U.S. Supreme Court as justices heard oral arguments in West Virginia v. B.P.J. Jan. 13, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
A potential Democratic majority on Capitol Hill would face a serious split over whether to use its newfound power to protect transgender Americans.

Progressive lawmakers are pushing Democratic leaders to undo President Donald Trump’s attacks on trans people’s health care, participation in athletics and protections against discrimination.

But affordability, not culture war fights, has been the overriding theme of Democrats’ push to retake control of Congress. Many centrists fear any pivot away from that pledge would splinter the party, especially with many Democratic candidates openly rejecting some trans rights initiatives during their campaigns.

“You have to focus on what people care about,” Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.) said in an interview. “Right now that’s affordability, and they want some relief. That’s what we should talk about.”

One senior House Democrat serving on House Appropriations, who was granted anonymity to discuss a private conversation, recalled personally asking Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries not to focus on trans issues or other flashpoints if the party wins the House.

Nearly a dozen lawmakers and advocates, however, argued for a two-pronged approach to protecting trans people: passing legislation to codify certain rights for trans individuals and using committee gavels to probe the Trump administration’s actions.

“We need to have an affirmative platform that protects and expands rights for LGBTQ people,” Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) said in an interview, while the Human Rights Campaign’s Ramiro Sarmiento said Congress “needs to use every tool it has to push back” on Trump.

Jeffries did not respond to a request for comment, but other top Democrats are responding to the conflict between affordability and civil rights by asking: Why not both?

“If we are telling people that we no longer value equality in this country, it's really hard to build a fair economy,” House Minority Whip Katherine Clark said in an interview. “You can't silo these issues out.”

What else we’re watching: 

— THE GOP'S SMALL DONOR PROBLEM: The GOP’s cash advantage over Democrats this cycle has been thanks to a small group of megadonors like Elon Musk. But when it comes to the grassroots donor base, there’s a stark contrast between the parties. Small donations through major online platforms have dipped for Republicans since 2022 while they're up for Democrats by about a third. That’s left vulnerable Republican candidates more reliant on Trump’s campaign war chest and super PACs.

— GOP CLIMATE BLOC FACES WIPEOUT: A midterm blue wave could decimate the cohort of Republicans who advocate for addressing climate change and pursuing clean-energy policies. The Conservative Climate Caucus, a House GOP group that pushes for those policies, could lose up to a third of its members in the midterms, with 11 of 66 members in tight races and another 15 retiring. That would shrink the pool of negotiating partners for Democrats as they plan on a renewed push for climate legislation.

CORRECTION: A previous version of this report misstated Rep. Tom Suozzi's party affiliation. He is a Democrat.

item.title: Democrats fracture on transgender rights as voters demand affordability focus
item.description: As candidates distance themselves, progressive lawmakers and advocates are pushing for action under future Democratic majorities.

media:content.media:title: “Congress needs to use every tool it has" to protect transgender Americans, one LGBTQ+ advocate said.

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Some Democrats are fired up to use their potential majorities in Congress next year and undo President Donald Trump’s attacks on transgender Americans. Others just want to focus on the cost of gas.

Ahead of the midterms, progressive lawmakers and congressional candidates are clashing with moderates in office and on the campaign trail over whether to pursue a legislative agenda that includes protecting trans people — whose health care, participation in athletics and protections against discrimination have been targeted by the administration.

“We need to have an affirmative platform that protects and expands rights for LGBTQ people,” said Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Ed Markey in an interview.

He is among nearly a dozen lawmakers and advocates who said they want Democrats to pursue a two-pronged approach: pass legislation to codify certain rights for trans individuals, and use committee gavels to compel public testimony from Trump officials on their efforts to undermine protections for trans and nonbinary people.

But the need to tackle affordability, not culture war fights, has been the overriding theme of the Democrats’ push to retake control of Congress. Many Democrats believe that their promise to lower the cost of living will be the reason they win back majorities in the House or the Senate.

Many centrists fear any pivot away from that pledge would splinter a new Democratic majority on Capitol Hill, especially with some candidates openly rejecting some trans rights initiatives during their campaigns.

“You have to focus on what people care about,” Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.) said in an interview. “Right now that’s affordability, and they want some relief. That’s what we should talk about.”

Rep. Marc Veasey, a moderate Texas Democrat who is retiring this year, said “cultural issues” including transgender rights are “something we should dive into once [Trump] is gone.”

“The American public is going to want to see our caucus focus on costs as long as he continues to affect the markets negatively with his tariffs and wars,” he said.

Progressive advocacy groups and their Hill allies say they can’t wait. Democrats, they argue, should hold hearings on the DOJ’s decision last summer to subpoena more than 20 doctors and clinics who’ve provided gender-affirming care to obtain potentially patient-identifying information, advocates say, leading some hospitals to stop providing youth gender affirming care.

They also want Democrats to challenge the Education Department’s move last month to officially rescind anti-discrimination protections for transgender students instituted under former President Joe Biden. They’re pushing, too, for an investigation of the Justice Department’s restrictions on gender-affirming care for incarcerated people and policy against placing prisoners in populations consistent with their gender identity — a move which has faced legal challenges.

In terms of legislation, Democrats are sure to encounter limitations so long as long as Trump is in office. The president is opposed to the cornerstone piece of LGBTQ+ advocates’ agenda, the Equality Act, which would amend civil rights laws to explicitly prohibit gender identity discrimination. It might not even have the votes to overcome a Senate filibuster and get to Trump’s desk.

Democrats likewise are sure to run into resistance in trying to attach pro-transgender policies to must-pass legislative vehicles, such as government spending bills or the annual defense policy package. The same goes for any attempts to overrule or modify the administration’s suggested changes to the 2030 Census, which include a proposal to remove questions about sexual orientation.
